The spotted coralgrouper (Plectropomus maculatus) is a commercially valuable serranid inhabiting coral reef ecosystems across the Indo-Pacific region. Field studies have documented that newly hatched, yolk-sac larvae emerging from pelagic eggs weigh approximately 0.00027 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00027 grams], a remarkably small initial mass that reflects the energetic constraints of planktotrophic development. The duration of the embryonic stage prior to eclosion is brief; at a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], hatching occurs roughly 8 days [ab = roughly 8 days] after fertilization. This rapid transition from fertilized ovum to free-swimming larva is characteristic of tropical serranids and allows individuals to quickly begin exploiting planktonic food resources. The small egg size, which correlates with the low wet weight at birth, is thought to be an adaptive response to the relatively high fecundity required in a pelagic environment where predation on early life stages is intense. Comparative data from related species indicate that this larval strategy trades off individual offspring provisioning for a larger number of propagules released per spawning event.

As juveniles transition into the demersal, reef-associated phase of their life cycle, they exhibit a substantial increase in somatic mass. Puberty, marking the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the initiation of gametogenesis, is reached when individuals attain a standard length of approximately 30 cm [Lp = approximately 30 cm]. The corresponding wet weight at puberty has been determined from length-weight regressions to be 359 grams [Wwp = 359 grams]. This size threshold appears to be a critical developmental milestone, after which energetic resources are increasingly partitioned toward reproductive tissues. The standard length at puberty is relatively modest compared to the ultimate total length of the species, suggesting that individuals become capable of participating in spawning aggregations well before they achieve their maximum somatic dimensions. This life-history pattern may enhance reproductive resilience, allowing younger, smaller fish to contribute to the population's breeding stock even as larger, more fecund individuals are targeted by fisheries.

Adult spotted coralgrouper can attain a very large ultimate total length of 125 cm [Li = 125 cm], making them one of the larger piscivores on Indo-Pacific coral reefs. The corresponding ultimate wet weight associated with this asymptotic length is 27,900 grams [Wwi = 27,900 grams]. These maximum values are typically observed in older, long-lived individuals that have successfully avoided predation and fishing mortality. The length-weight relationship used to derive this asymptotic mass underscores the robust, deep-bodied morphology of the species. Such a large body size confers a competitive advantage in capturing prey and defending territories, but it also implies a protracted growth period to reach these upper limits. Population surveys often note that individuals exceeding 100 cm in total length are increasingly rare, likely due to high fishing pressure on the largest size classes in many parts of their geographic range. The species' life span is consequently a critical factor in determining how many individuals can achieve these ultimate dimensions.

Longevity studies based on otolith increment analysis have revealed that the maximum recorded life span for Plectropomus maculatus is 9,490 days [am = 9,490 days] when maintained under ambient thermal conditions of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This translates to an exceptional 26 years in the wild, placing the spotted coralgrouper among the longer-lived serranids. Temperature appears to play a modulating role in the rate of senescence; the life span estimate is specifically tied to the thermal regime of the coral reef environment. Such extended longevity has important implications for population dynamics, as older individuals contribute disproportionately to the reproductive output of the stock across multiple spawning seasons. The combination of a large ultimate size and a long life span suggests a life-history strategy that buffers against years of poor recruitment, a common pattern among reef fishes that experience highly variable early-life survival. However, this strategy also renders the species particularly vulnerable to overfishing, as the removal of large, old individuals can take decades to replace.

Reproductive output in this species is substantial, reflecting the high fecundity typical of broadcast-spawning epinephelids. Under optimal conditions at a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], a mature female produces approximately 8,219 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 8,219 eggs per day] throughout the spawning season. This daily fecundity is a product of the species' high spawning frequency and its large clutch size. The maximum reproduction rate, when integrated over the entire spawning period, results in a massive annual reproductive potential that helps offset the high mortality experienced during the pelagic larval phase. The temperature dependence of this rate is notable; at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], metabolic processes are optimized for gamete production and the energetic costs of spawning are minimized. Comparative studies of serranid reproduction indicate that such high fecundity is common among species that form large spawning aggregations, as the synchronous release of gametes by many individuals enhances fertilization success in the water column. Fisheries management strategies for this species must account for this reproductive potential to set sustainable catch limits.
